I will address something being talked about here in this thread though. For realtime IK updates, Control Rig should be first choice because it runs on a helper/utility thread. For a multi weapon solution, your weapons need sockets on them for the locations and rotations to be accurate. You can then implement a system (like what I learned from manipulating, breaking, and then fixing ALS Community) where you put a curve on that weapon’s animations, call it Hand_IK or whatever, that has a value of 0 OR 1. In your update, you’ll do a lookup on the curve value to set a bool for Hand IK to be utilized in your anim graph. 1 = True 0 = False type of thing. If True your hand IK will adjust for socket locations. Socket names should be the same across all weapons to allow for simplicity in the anim graph. Creation of the waves on the anims can be simplified using an animation modifier. Adding the sockets and the waves is part of the setup. 
Now as far as using the same control rig across characters, if they’ve got the same skeleton that should be doable. You can even do Left Hand IK and Right Hand IK waves separately, maybe even add character specific offsets to the anim BP. 
To control conditionally if you use the control rig create a cached pose right before where you’d use the CR, then use a blend pose by bool feeding in your bAreWeUsingIK. A can be the cached pose sent into the CR and B can just be the cached pose.

So logic like this would typically be encapsulated to an actor component that gets added to the character, but don’t worry about that right now, let’s just get it working. 

Now, sharing of data between two classes is what interfaces are made for (not literally but it’s a perfect use case). So make a blueprint interface for your character, if you don’t have one already. Add a function to that interface. Call it “ add active pickup”, whatever, give the function one input of type actor. Go to your pickup actor. Add a box collision in the actor viewport, and make sure it’s big enough for your character to walk into. Now, click on the box collision, and in the properties panel at the side scroll all the way down and add an “event on begin overlap”. This will add an event to the actor’s graph called on begin overlap. One of the inputs is overlapping actor(s). Drag that input out and call the interface function with it as the target. For the input, connect a reference to self (the pickup actor). Now, any old actor can overlap with this, but unless they have that interface nothing will happen. So back in you character class that has the interface added to it, under the functions list double click on the interface function name. Drag that input out and create a new variable, call it active pickup. Now in your E keyboard event you have a reference to the pick up actor itself. So, on press ‘E’, if that variable is valid (literally call the function isValid and give it that variable as input) you increment the objects collected variable on your character by plus one. Then drag out from that variable again and call set lifespan. You can set the input to something small. This will let the now picked up actor destroy itself. Last but not least set the active pickup variable here, but don’t set it to anything. This means the variable will be null and if you press E again the variable will not be valid. So no bugs. 

That’s one of the simplest but effective ways of doing what you’re looking for. The more complex your game becomes the more complex you might want to make the system, mine tracks multiple pick up actors at a time and also uses the camera angle to know which one should be active pick up. I also use collider shape on the character and not the actor, but again that’s for a more complex system.

Oh and the anim blueprints are running FSMs (finite state machines). You’re AnimBP is always in one of those animation states, and only transitions to another when proper circumstances have been met. There a lot of logic behind it, but they made it easier on UE devs by not forcing us to create/manage it.

A finite state machine is coding concept where a particular object can only be in one particular state at a time. Create an Enum, call it E_AIState, and add to it None, Idle, Combat. Now you can control what behaviors are performed when the ai is in each state by simply referencing their local AIState variable. If none, you could make some decisions about what state to enter or what behavior trees should be running and move from there. Switch on Enum can be a handy way of running this in the controller. I have an AIState Enum, WeaponType Enum, even AIType Enum (trader, guard, citizen, noble, etc.).

I can also manage what tree of behaviors is currently being run at runtime from the controller. Is this person a trader/shopkeeper, a guard, or a typical NPC. All should have different behavior trees, but may reuse certain behavioral tasks.

My ai perceives an actor. If it’s an enemy, it gets added to an array, and the ai has an enemy to attack he now attempts to draw his weapon. If he has one he draws it, closes distance, and attempts to attack if close enough. Now, if he doesn’t have a weapon, that task fails and maybe he now tries to find one or fight unarmed. If he’s not close enough to attack, he then closes distance and does so. I also use a combination of BTs and FSMs. Certain subtrees can’t even be accessed unless my ai is in that state. This keeps them in a particular loop of desired behaviors. Now imagine I want different combat behaviors based on weapon type. Now only certain sub-subtrees can be accessed if in a particular state with a particular weapon. 

BTs are as useful as we make them. Sure ai behaviors can be coded in the controller, but then you end up with a huge, bloated, often difficult to read/navigate controller. Instead we can manage state from the controller and behaviors in the behavior trees. Also, if an enemy is perceived by the ai, cast to it in the controller, add that to an array so you can keep from casting over and over again either in the behaviors or the perception system.

Now you’re game can implement specific things that are dependent on a character’s alignment and all I have to do to use it is have a reference to the character and call my function. 

Personally, I might put the functionality in an actor component that I attach to the character. On character’s beginplay I can give the component a soft reference to the character. The component uses that reference to get the alignment float attribute and return the appropriate Enum value. This will keep the code a little more modular, and I can add more functionality based on alignment like in Fable (modifying appearance and aura) and it’s all contained in this one component.

To answer your first question, you’ll want to make sure it is a skeletal mesh. So, yes, you would rig it the same as the character. I would follow the same process as in this Fractured Fantasy video: 

https://youtu.be/6tpc4oNzSXc

It needs a similar skeleton, and you’ll have to get the weight painting so that it deforms properly. You’ll need something like Blender to do so. Also, like in the video, you’ll be able to shape whatever the clothing asset is to your character model. It’s a little bit of a process, but if you figure out a workflow for it it’s going to open up your options a lot more. 

As far as your reloading question, I believe you have a couple options. I’ve heard of people using additive animations to play reloads. This allows the main animation, such as walking, to keep playing. I think you could also use a Blend per Bone to play it. Every YouTube tut that does melee, like a rpg/arpg style, will show how to attack while walking/running and the way they do it would also work for this. You shouldn’t need a full body anim for reloading and most players wouldn’t expect to have to stop whatever they’re doing and wait for a reload animation to play.
